oneLine: Help a laboratory turn a superconducting material claim into a repeatable measurement and a clear engineering decision.
need: A promising material headline does not tell a founder whether a sample can carry useful current, survive repeated cooling or be manufactured consistently. This concept gives materials teams and potential customers a common test record before anyone designs an entire product around an uncertain result.
offer: Develop a measurement and comparison service for a tightly defined superconducting use case. Begin with sample provenance, a chosen operating temperature and the customer's actual requirements. The proposed enterprise would organise independent testing and explain what each result permits the team to claim.
users: University materials groups preparing a reproducibility study
Instrument developers comparing candidate components
Founders who need an independent technical review

firstPilot.title: A repeatable sample comparison
steps: Choose one established reference sample and one candidate with a qualified laboratory.
Agree how temperature, applied field, current and sample preparation will be recorded.
Repeat the measurement with a second operator and include failed runs.
Produce a decision brief that separates an observed transition from the requirements of a useful device.
firstPilot.deliverable: A traceable sample register, measurement files and a customer-specific decision brief.

evidence.known: Superconductivity is an established phenomenon; the proposed venture and any candidate material still require their own evidence.
evidence.unknown: The source does not identify a material, operating envelope, laboratory partner or reproducible advantage.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Repeat the selected reference measurement and quantify how much results vary between runs.

resources: A qualified materials laboratory and suitable measurement equipment
A technical founder who can explain uncertainty
Customer interviews centred on one device requirement
businessModel: A proposed paid testing and technical interpretation service, followed by a product only if a customer can show a valuable and repeatable advantage.
leadershipDecision: Choose who has authority to reject a headline claim, and give the testing lead independence from the fundraising story.
risks: A magnetic response alone may be over-interpreted.
Cooling and manufacturing requirements may outweigh the material benefit.
A proprietary sample may prevent independent replication.
title: Superconductors
sourceNote: Developed from original enterprise 61 in the 500 Queens VC NEW Long presentation (slide 17) and the planning document (page 8). This expanded brief is a proposed development path, not evidence of an operating venture or a confirmed partner.
equalityQuestions: Can women in regional areas access the laboratory and technical mentoring?
Who receives credit and ownership for careful replication work?

oneLine: Design useful polymers around a real product's life, repair and recovery needs.
need: A material can look ideal in a small demonstration and still fail when exposed to heat, salt, repeated handling or an ordinary repair. Small manufacturers need a way to choose materials using the conditions their products actually face, including what happens after use.
offer: Create a materials selection and prototyping studio for one product family such as reusable containers, workshop housings or coastal equipment covers. Compare candidate polymers with the existing material, documenting durability, production requirements and realistic recovery routes rather than treating every new formulation as automatically sustainable.
users: Small manufacturers replacing a troublesome plastic part
Repair businesses seeking consistent replacement materials
Community ventures designing products for coastal conditions

firstPilot.title: One part, three material choices
steps: Ask a willing maker to nominate a part that repeatedly fails.
Record the actual loads, cleaning routine, exposure and expected service life.
Make comparable prototypes through an appropriate workshop or supplier.
Test the same failure conditions and ask the people who use the part to handle each version.
Check with a real recovery operator whether the proposed material can enter an available collection stream.
firstPilot.deliverable: A part specification, comparison samples and a decision on the most useful next material trial.

evidence.known: The first service can use available materials and fabrication methods; it does not depend on inventing a new polymer.
evidence.unknown: The original suggestion specifies no formulation, product, durability target or recycling arrangement.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Measure the failure mode that matters to the chosen customer using a consistent comparison.

resources: A manufacturing or polymer specialist
Access to a suitable prototyping workshop
A willing customer and a recovery operator
businessModel: Project fees for selection and prototyping, with supply or licensing considered only after the part performs as required.
leadershipDecision: Decide whether the venture's advantage is a material formulation, a better part design or independent advice; each needs different skills and ownership.
risks: A recyclable label may not match local recovery capacity.
Additives can change performance and handling requirements.
A prototype's production method may not transfer to volume manufacturing.
title: Polymers
sourceNote: Developed from original enterprise 62 in the 500 Queens VC NEW Long presentation (slide 17) and the planning document (page 8). This expanded brief is a proposed development path, not evidence of an operating venture or a confirmed partner.
equalityQuestions: Does the product fit bodies and routines beyond a single assumed user?
Who carries the cleaning, repair and end-of-life work?

oneLine: Turn the ambition of perfect crystals into a disciplined service for controlling and measuring defects.
need: A crystal's usefulness depends on the property needed by a particular device. A beautiful sample is not automatically a reliable sensor, optical component or computing material. Founders need clear links between growth conditions, defects and an application before they can justify a specialised production process.
offer: Develop a small crystal-growth and characterisation programme around one chosen material. The original word 'perfect' is an ambition, not a promised product property. The service would deliver measured samples, process records and an honest account of variability that another laboratory can inspect.
users: Photonics researchers needing consistent sample properties
Sensor developers testing a defined crystal component
Teaching laboratories building practical materials skills

firstPilot.title: A reproducible growth record
steps: Select one accessible material and a reference growth method with a laboratory supervisor.
Write the sample acceptance criteria before beginning a run.
Record preparation, growth conditions and handling in a common log.
Compare successive samples with suitable characterisation methods.
Have another operator repeat the process and document any differences.
firstPilot.deliverable: A labelled sample set and process record connecting measured defects to the selected use case.

evidence.known: Crystal growth and characterisation are established disciplines. No defect-free production process is claimed here.
evidence.unknown: The source gives no target material, growth route, yield or application-specific quality requirement.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Compare the same chosen property across separately grown samples.

resources: A materials laboratory and qualified supervisor
Characterisation access matched to the intended property
Reliable sample storage and documentation
businessModel: A proposed specialist sample and characterisation service, with repeat supply dependent on verified consistency and customer demand.
leadershipDecision: Make the quality standard a customer and laboratory decision. Do not let the evocative title become an acceptance criterion nobody can measure.
risks: A useful surface measurement may conceal internal defects.
Growth conditions can be difficult to reproduce.
A narrow market may not support dedicated equipment.
title: Perfect Crystal Growth
sourceNote: Developed from original enterprise 63 in the 500 Queens VC NEW Long presentation (slide 17) and the planning document (page 8). This expanded brief is a proposed development path, not evidence of an operating venture or a confirmed partner.
equalityQuestions: Can new researchers access the instruments and training needed to challenge results?
Are technicians and sample preparers included in credit and ownership?

oneLine: Build durable ceramic components by starting with one demanding local use.
need: Heat, abrasion and corrosion can make ordinary parts expensive to replace. Ceramics may offer a useful alternative, but a brittle failure or difficult attachment can create a new problem. A small enterprise needs to understand the whole assembly and the people maintaining it.
offer: Create a design and testing practice for ceramic inserts, protective parts or functional surfaces. Work with existing suppliers first, comparing an available ceramic option with the current component. Custom compositions would come later, if a specific unmet requirement justifies the research.
users: Equipment maintainers replacing worn components
Makers developing small production runs
Technical teams seeking independent component comparisons

firstPilot.title: A replaceable wear component
steps: Choose an accessible non-critical component with a documented wear problem.
Record its dimensions, attachment, loading and maintenance routine.
Ask a qualified supplier to propose an existing ceramic alternative.
Trial a suitable prototype under controlled conditions before field use.
Compare wear, breakage, installation effort and replacement practicality with the current part.
firstPilot.deliverable: A component drawing, inspection record and go-or-stop recommendation for a limited field trial.

evidence.known: Commercial ceramics can be assessed for a specific part without claiming a new material breakthrough.
evidence.unknown: No composition, operating environment or customer requirement is specified in the original suggestion.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Measure wear and cracking using the same exposure and inspection method for both options.

resources: A component designer and ceramic supplier
A workshop able to make a suitable mounting assembly
Customer maintenance records and a controlled test arrangement
businessModel: Design and comparison fees could lead to supply of a proven replacement component, with the maintenance case made explicit.
leadershipDecision: Choose an application where the team can inspect failures safely and learn quickly. Assign ownership of installation guidance and quality checks.
risks: Brittle fracture can defeat an apparently strong material.
Joining a ceramic to another material can dominate the design.
A low-volume part may have unattractive production costs.
title: Ceramics
sourceNote: Developed from original enterprise 64 in the 500 Queens VC NEW Long presentation (slide 17) and the planning document (page 8). This expanded brief is a proposed development path, not evidence of an operating venture or a confirmed partner.
equalityQuestions: Can women doing maintenance influence the part design?
Will regional users be able to obtain and replace the component?

oneLine: Compare battery electrode ideas against a defined storage job and a full test record.
need: A new electrode is only one part of a storage system. A founder needs to understand repeatability, processing, degradation and the conditions of the intended job. Reporting a single impressive result can hide the practical constraints that determine whether a customer can use the material.
offer: Develop a supervised electrode evaluation service for one chemistry and one application. The programme would connect material preparation to comparable cell measurements, recording the assumptions required before moving from laboratory samples to a larger product.
users: Materials researchers seeking application feedback
Storage developers screening electrode candidates
Manufacturing teams exploring a process improvement

firstPilot.title: A controlled electrode comparison
steps: Choose a reference electrode and one candidate with a qualified battery laboratory.
Agree the cell configuration, preparation method and comparison protocol.
Record all samples, including those that fail preparation or testing.
Compare the relevant performance across repeated cycles and independent samples.
Review the result with a potential customer whose storage needs are clearly described.
firstPilot.deliverable: A reproducible comparison report and a list of unresolved steps before larger cell development.

evidence.known: Electrode testing is an established laboratory activity; this proposal does not establish a new battery's performance.
evidence.unknown: The source identifies no chemistry, manufacturing route, verified result or customer application.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Determine whether the candidate's result repeats across independently prepared samples under the agreed protocol.

resources: A qualified battery laboratory with appropriate containment
A materials and process specialist
A customer brief describing the actual storage duty
businessModel: Contract evaluation and development work, with licensing or component supply only after a defendable technical advantage is established.
leadershipDecision: Give the laboratory lead responsibility for the comparison protocol and publication of limitations before discussing product claims.
risks: Results from small cells may not transfer to production.
Preparation differences can overwhelm a material comparison.
A promising electrode may depend on an impractical electrolyte or supply chain.
title: Anodes and Cathodes
sourceNote: Developed from original enterprise 65 in the 500 Queens VC NEW Long presentation (slide 17) and the planning document (page 8). This expanded brief is a proposed development path, not evidence of an operating venture or a confirmed partner.
equalityQuestions: Are women represented in technical decisions and manufacturing roles?
Who bears the handling and end-of-life workload across the proposed supply chain?

oneLine: Investigate the electrolyte as part of a complete, clearly defined energy-storage system.
need: The material between electrodes affects how a cell is made, operated and maintained. A formulation that performs in one arrangement can behave differently with another electrode or temperature range. Small teams need evidence about compatibility rather than a generic claim of a better battery.
offer: Build an electrolyte comparison and documentation service with a qualified laboratory. Focus on an identified problem such as process consistency or performance over the customer's required operating conditions. Use a reference formulation and agreed measurements so every claimed improvement has a meaningful baseline.
users: Battery research teams comparing formulations
Developers evaluating compatibility with an electrode
Manufacturers investigating a repeatability problem

firstPilot.title: One compatibility question
steps: Write the exact cell chemistry and operating problem with the customer.
Choose a reference formulation and a controlled candidate through a qualified laboratory.
Document preparation, storage, impurities and sample history.
Compare relevant behaviour across the same operating conditions.
Record handling and end-of-test requirements in the technical handover.
firstPilot.deliverable: A compatibility matrix, sample history and evidence brief for the next cell-development decision.

evidence.known: Electrolyte properties can be measured within a defined system; this page proposes a research service rather than a finished cell.
evidence.unknown: No formulation, compatible electrode pair or verified advantage is supplied by the source.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Test whether the candidate resolves the stated compatibility problem under repeated, controlled conditions.

resources: A qualified electrochemistry team
Laboratory facilities suited to the chosen materials
A customer with a specific cell-development question
businessModel: Paid formulation screening or collaborative development, with intellectual-property arrangements agreed before samples are exchanged.
leadershipDecision: Decide which measurements the customer needs and who can use the resulting data. Protect the independence of the technical conclusion.
risks: Formulations may be sensitive to contamination or storage.
Performance in a test cell may conceal manufacturing constraints.
Handling and recovery requirements may limit an otherwise attractive material.
title: Electrolytes
sourceNote: Developed from original enterprise 66 in the 500 Queens VC NEW Long presentation (slide 17) and the planning document (page 8). This expanded brief is a proposed development path, not evidence of an operating venture or a confirmed partner.
equalityQuestions: Can production workers influence the formulation and handling brief?
Does the business model recognise laboratory and quality-control work fairly?

oneLine: Use carefully shaped resonators to solve one measurable sensing, vibration or signal problem.
need: Resonance is useful only when its behaviour matches an intended job. A component can work beautifully in isolation and shift when mounted, heated or touched. Customers need a design that remains useful in the environment where they will actually use it.
offer: Form a design and prototyping service for one class of resonator, beginning with accessible mechanical or acoustic devices. Compare shapes, materials and mounting arrangements. More demanding optical or electronic applications would require their own specialist team and measurement plan.
users: Equipment designers managing an unwanted vibration
Instrument makers developing a sensing element
Learning programmes needing a tangible physics demonstrator

firstPilot.title: A resonator that survives its mounting
steps: Select one customer problem and the physical quantity to measure.
Build a reference component and a small set of alternative geometries.
Measure the response before and after installing each component in its intended mount.
Repeat under the relevant environmental changes.
Explain the useful operating range and failure conditions in plain language.
firstPilot.deliverable: A demonstrator, response measurements and a mounting specification that another maker can reproduce.

evidence.known: A constrained resonator experiment can use established measurement and fabrication tools.
evidence.unknown: The source does not specify whether the venture concerns mechanical, acoustic, electrical or optical resonance.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Compare how the chosen response changes between the free component and its installed state.

resources: A designer with the relevant physics knowledge
Fabrication access and suitable measurement instruments
A customer or educator who can trial the demonstrator
businessModel: Project fees for design and measurement, followed by a component kit or specialist service if demand repeats.
leadershipDecision: Select a single physical domain for the first team. Set a clear boundary between a teaching demonstration and a qualified industrial component.
risks: Environmental sensitivity may overwhelm the intended signal.
Mounting and manufacturing variation can change behaviour.
A narrow peak response may be less useful than a robust wider operating range.
title: Resonators
sourceNote: Developed from original enterprise 67 in the 500 Queens VC NEW Long presentation (slide 17) and the planning document (page 8). This expanded brief is a proposed development path, not evidence of an operating venture or a confirmed partner.
equalityQuestions: Can learners with different access needs observe and operate the demonstrator?
Who defines a useful measurement: the designer or the person using it?

oneLine: Translate the ambition of an absolute vacuum into measurable vacuum engineering and leak control.
need: A useful vacuum system is defined by its pressure, cleanliness, leakage and ability to repeat an experiment. 'Absolute vacuum' is an ideal, not a deliverable that this network can promise. Laboratories and specialist makers may instead need better records, fixtures and fault-finding around practical vacuum equipment.
offer: Develop a vacuum readiness and troubleshooting service with a qualified technical partner. Start by documenting one existing chamber, its instrumentation and the experiment it supports. The venture's value would be in repeatability and understandable operating records, not an impossible claim of removing every particle.
users: Research groups with inconsistent chamber behaviour
Instrument developers preparing a vacuum-dependent prototype
Technical educators building a supervised demonstration

firstPilot.title: A chamber with a trustworthy history
steps: Select an existing supervised system and identify its required operating condition.
Record chamber materials, connections, instruments and maintenance history.
Establish a baseline pressure history using suitable calibrated instruments.
Investigate one known source of leakage or contamination with the technical lead.
Repeat the baseline and document what changed and what remains unexplained.
firstPilot.deliverable: A system map, pressure record and maintenance brief tied to one experiment.

evidence.known: Practical vacuum engineering concerns measurable conditions; the original absolute language is treated as an aspiration.
evidence.unknown: The source gives no chamber, target pressure, instrument specification or demonstrated result.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Compare the chamber's pressure history before and after one controlled intervention.

resources: A qualified vacuum engineer or laboratory technician
An existing appropriate chamber and instrumentation
A documented experiment whose needs can be expressed clearly
businessModel: Proposed inspection, documentation and engineering support fees, with equipment development justified only by repeated customer problems.
leadershipDecision: Replace vague extreme-performance language with a measurable acceptance condition that the team and customer can both inspect.
risks: Instrument limits can be confused with the absence of gas.
Unrecorded material or maintenance changes can invalidate comparisons.
Specialist equipment and service needs may limit a local market.
title: Absolute Vacuums
sourceNote: Developed from original enterprise 68 in the 500 Queens VC NEW Long presentation (slide 17) and the planning document (page 8). This expanded brief is a proposed development path, not evidence of an operating venture or a confirmed partner.
equalityQuestions: Can women entering technical trades gain meaningful supervised roles?
Are maintenance knowledge and patient fault-finding recognised as leadership skills?

oneLine: Make laser precision meaningful by connecting it to a specific measurement or manufacturing task.
need: Precision can mean position, timing, wavelength, stability or repeatability. Without a defined job, the phrase 'extremely precise' tells a customer very little. Small engineering teams need help choosing which quantity matters and whether an available instrument already meets the need.
offer: Create an optical measurement and integration practice with an experienced photonics partner. Begin with a non-public, supervised laboratory application and compare an existing system against a clear requirement. Develop new hardware only when the evidence shows why integration alone is insufficient.
users: Researchers with a repeatability problem
Manufacturers comparing optical inspection options
Instrument teams preparing an independent verification plan

firstPilot.title: Specify the precision before buying the laser
steps: Choose one task and define the quantity that must remain stable.
Document the current instrument and relevant environmental conditions.
Create a repeatable measurement sequence with the laboratory lead.
Compare the result with the customer's acceptance condition.
Separate instrument behaviour from mounting, software and operator effects.
firstPilot.deliverable: A requirements sheet, repeatability dataset and recommendation on the next integration step.

evidence.known: Photonics offers established tools for precision work; the source supplies no new laser design or measured advantage.
evidence.unknown: The intended application, wavelength, stability requirement and technical team remain open.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Measure repeatability of the chosen quantity under the customer's relevant conditions.

resources: A qualified photonics specialist and suitable controlled facility
Calibrated instruments appropriate to the claim
A customer with a measurable task and an existing baseline
businessModel: Technical specification and integration fees could support a specialist instrument product if the same unmet need appears across customers.
leadershipDecision: Choose a clear application and name the person responsible for measurement quality and supervised operation.
risks: A precise source does not ensure a precise assembled system.
Environmental drift can be mistaken for a hardware defect.
Specialist handling and facility requirements may dominate delivery.
title: Extremely Precise Lasers
sourceNote: Developed from original enterprise 69 in the 500 Queens VC NEW Long presentation (slide 17) and the planning document (page 8). This expanded brief is a proposed development path, not evidence of an operating venture or a confirmed partner.
equalityQuestions: Can regional users access the specialist service without owning expensive equipment?
Who gets to question the precision claim before a purchase decision?

oneLine: Explore magnetic control through an observable engineering demonstration with explicit limits.
need: Magnetic levitation attracts attention, but a useful application also needs stability, load handling, control and reliable recovery when conditions change. A founder needs to know whether magnetic support solves a customer's problem better than a conventional mechanical arrangement.
offer: Develop a supervised magnetic positioning or demonstration platform around a small, defined load. Compare its controllability and maintenance needs with a simple alternative. The first commercial possibility could be education or specialist testing, while larger transport or industrial claims remain outside the pilot.
users: Educators seeking an engaging control-systems demonstrator
Instrument developers studying non-contact positioning
Makers comparing support mechanisms for a specialised object

firstPilot.title: A controlled non-contact demonstration
steps: Choose a modest demonstrator with an experienced electrical or mechanical engineer.
Write down the supported load, motion limits and intended interruption behaviour.
Build the measurement and control arrangement before tuning for visual effect.
Record stability and recovery under agreed disturbances.
Invite a prospective user to explain whether the demonstration helps their work or learning.
firstPilot.deliverable: An instrumented prototype, operating record and comparison with a conventional support.

evidence.known: Magnetic control is an established engineering area; the proposal does not claim a new force, unlimited lift or a complete transport system.
evidence.unknown: The original suggestion gives no configuration, load, control method or validated use case.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Record position stability and recovery for the agreed load across repeated disturbances.

resources: An experienced controls and hardware team
Suitable instruments and a supervised workspace
A user willing to evaluate the actual demonstration
businessModel: A proposed teaching kit or specialist test service, with a larger product considered only when a customer requirement supports it.
leadershipDecision: Keep the prototype's educational or engineering purpose visible. Assign one technical lead responsibility for claims and operating limits.
risks: A visually impressive effect may lack a useful customer application.
Power, heat and control requirements can dominate the design.
A small demonstrator may not scale to a larger load.
title: Extreme Magnetism or Levitation
sourceNote: Developed from original enterprise 70 in the 500 Queens VC NEW Long presentation (slide 17) and the planning document (page 8). This expanded brief is a proposed development path, not evidence of an operating venture or a confirmed partner.
equalityQuestions: Can the demonstrator be used by people with different mobility and reach?
Are women given control-system and engineering leadership roles?

oneLine: Design spacewear around the movement, fit and dignity of many different bodies.
need: A 'second skin' space suit is a demanding engineering ambition. The practical starting point is understanding how garments and equipment interact with real people: different heights, bust sizes, body mass, mobility, reach and ways of dressing. A suit concept cannot assume every wearer shares a single athletic shape.
offer: Build an inclusive fit and movement research studio for future spacewear. Start with non-pressurised mock-ups, not protective equipment. Explore fastening, adjustment, layering and the ability to complete tasks independently, then hand a traceable requirements brief to experienced suit engineers.
users: Human-factors researchers and specialist garment designers
Space training teams exploring task ergonomics
Women whose bodies are poorly represented in conventional equipment sizing

firstPilot.title: A movement and fit workshop
steps: Recruit consenting adult participants with varied body shapes and access needs.
Let participants choose practical tasks and describe existing equipment frustrations.
Make adjustable non-protective mock-ups and test reach, dressing and comfort.
Record participant feedback without publishing personal measurements.
Ask a qualified human-factors specialist to translate findings into design requirements.
firstPilot.deliverable: A participant-reviewed fit brief and non-protective garment demonstrator.

evidence.known: Human-factors and garment studies can inform a future suit; the pilot would not establish pressure protection or flight readiness.
evidence.unknown: No material, pressure system, thermal design or qualified engineering partner is specified in the original concept.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Compare task completion and wearer-reported fit across the agreed mock-up variations.

resources: A garment designer and human-factors lead
Paid participant involvement and accessible workshop space
A specialist space engineering reviewer
businessModel: Contract fit research and development services could precede any specialised garment product.
leadershipDecision: Give wearers authority over what comfort and independence mean. Ensure larger and large-busted women influence the initial design, rather than being added as an afterthought.
risks: A comfortable mock-up may not work as a pressure garment.
Personal body measurements need careful participant control.
A glamorous illustration can conceal unresolved fit and engineering questions.
title: Second Skin Space Suits
sourceNote: Developed from original enterprise 71 in the 500 Queens VC NEW Long presentation (slide 17) and the planning document (page 8). This expanded brief is a proposed development path, not evidence of an operating venture or a confirmed partner.
equalityQuestions: Would a large-busted, fat or differently mobile woman have equal influence over the suit design?
Can wearers choose privacy around body measurements and fitting?

oneLine: Make radiation protection decisions traceable to an exposure scenario and evidence.
need: Space radiation protection is a system problem involving the environment, mission, materials and people. A material image or dramatic shield concept cannot establish protection. A useful enterprise would help teams compare options without losing the assumptions behind a reassuring diagram.
offer: Develop a research and engineering comparison service with qualified radiation specialists. Define a single mission scenario, examine published measurements and identify what a candidate material or layout still needs to demonstrate. The first product would be a transparent decision tool, not a protective claim.
users: Habitat designers comparing candidate layouts
Materials researchers preparing a test proposal
Educators explaining the limits of space protection concepts

firstPilot.title: One exposure scenario, explicit assumptions
steps: Select a bounded published mission scenario with a specialist reviewer.
List the radiation environment and protection question without inventing missing inputs.
Compare a reference shielding arrangement with one proposed alternative.
Record model assumptions and separate simulated outputs from measured evidence.
Create a laboratory test brief for the uncertainty that most affects the conclusion.
firstPilot.deliverable: An assumption register, comparison model and independently reviewable test brief.

evidence.known: NASA treats radiation as a significant human-spaceflight research challenge. This concept provides no validated shielding product.
evidence.unknown: The source gives no material, exposure scenario, model validation or tested protection result.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Have a qualified team identify and measure the candidate property required to test the selected model.

resources: A radiation protection specialist
Relevant published mission and material data
Access to appropriate modelling expertise and independent review
businessModel: Proposed research, modelling and test-planning contracts, with component development conditional on independent evidence.
leadershipDecision: Name the person who can stop a protection claim from being published when the evidence does not support it.
risks: Results depend on the radiation environment and geometry.
An attractive material may add impractical mass or integration demands.
Simulation output can be mistaken for demonstrated protection.
title: Radiation Protection Systems
sourceNote: Developed from original enterprise 72 in the 500 Queens VC NEW Long presentation (slide 17) and the planning document (page 8). This expanded brief is a proposed development path, not evidence of an operating venture or a confirmed partner.
equalityQuestions: Does the exposure scenario represent the bodies and working patterns of the intended crew?
Who can challenge a reassuring protection claim before it is used in design?

oneLine: Support contamination-response planning with accountable records and specialist-led evidence.
need: The original remediation idea needs a clear distinction between detecting contamination, containing it and actually removing it. A general-purpose technology story can blur those jobs. Organisations dealing with a contaminated environment need qualified operators and traceable evidence of what happened to the material.
offer: Create a documentation and remote-inspection concept for a specialist remediation team. The first pilot would use a harmless training scenario to practise mapping, sample records, equipment handover and chain of responsibility. It would not process radioactive material or claim a treatment method.
users: Qualified remediation organisations improving field documentation
Robotics teams developing remote inspection interfaces
Training providers using controlled non-hazardous exercises

firstPilot.title: A harmless remediation rehearsal
steps: Ask a qualified specialist to define a fictional training site and required records.
Use clearly labelled safe substitutes to represent materials and samples.
Test how the team records locations, handovers, uncertainty and unresolved areas.
Practise a change in conditions and check whether the records remain understandable.
Have an independent reviewer reconstruct the exercise from the final documentation.
firstPilot.deliverable: A training workflow and evidence package showing whether the work can be reconstructed reliably.

evidence.known: Documentation and remote-inspection workflows can be trialled without hazardous material. No radiation-removal mechanism is established here.
evidence.unknown: The original suggestion names no contaminant, treatment process, authorised operator or site.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Check how many sample and location histories the independent reviewer can reconstruct without asking the original team.

resources: A qualified remediation adviser
A safe training environment and labelled substitutes
A field-documentation designer and willing training team
businessModel: Proposed training, workflow design and technical documentation services for established specialist operators.
leadershipDecision: Keep operational authority with qualified remediation professionals and make the proposed venture's supporting role explicit.
risks: A rehearsal may omit difficult field conditions.
Poor records can make it impossible to verify the destination of material.
An inspection result can be wrongly presented as proof of successful remediation.
title: Radiation Remediation Systems
sourceNote: Developed from original enterprise 73 in the 500 Queens VC NEW Long presentation (slide 17) and the planning document (page 8). This expanded brief is a proposed development path, not evidence of an operating venture or a confirmed partner.
equalityQuestions: Are women in field and documentation roles included in the rehearsal design?
Who receives support, training and authority when the exercise exposes a gap?

oneLine: Connect metal printing and welding to parts that customers can inspect, repair and trust.
need: A complex printed shape is not automatically a useful component. Customers need dimensional accuracy, material consistency, finishing, inspection and a credible repair route. For a new venture, an ordinary part with a clear problem is a better learning opportunity than an unqualified flight-critical claim.
offer: Build a metal prototyping and process comparison service with an established fabrication partner. Compare printing, welding and conventional manufacture for one non-critical part. The enterprise would explain which method best serves the customer and document the result so another fabricator can understand it.
users: Small manufacturers needing a difficult low-volume part
Repair businesses assessing whether a replacement is practical
Researchers exploring fabrication trade-offs

firstPilot.title: One part through alternative processes
steps: Choose a non-critical component with a willing customer and fabrication specialist.
Define dimensions, service conditions, inspection needs and the current manufacturing method.
Obtain comparable prototypes or quotations through suitable processes.
Inspect the produced parts and record finishing and rework.
Review the whole delivery path with the person who installs or maintains the component.
firstPilot.deliverable: A process comparison, inspected prototype and customer decision on the next production step.

evidence.known: Existing fabrication services can support a bounded comparison. This concept does not establish flight-qualified manufacturing.
evidence.unknown: The source provides no target alloy, process, part specification or demonstrated production capability.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Compare the completed part against its agreed dimensional and inspection requirements.

resources: A qualified fabrication partner
A designer and suitable inspection capability
A customer who can explain the part's service conditions
businessModel: Design, coordination and inspection fees could lead to a repeat component service or specialised production capability.
leadershipDecision: Choose whether to own equipment or coordinate skilled partners. Put inspection authority alongside production authority from the first job.
risks: Post-processing can erase an apparent production advantage.
Internal defects may require specialist inspection.
Equipment ownership may precede sufficient repeat demand.
title: 3D Metallic Printers/Welders
sourceNote: Developed from original enterprise 74 in the 500 Queens VC NEW Long presentation (slide 17) and the planning document (page 8). This expanded brief is a proposed development path, not evidence of an operating venture or a confirmed partner.
equalityQuestions: Can women access fabrication, inspection and ownership roles in the venture?
Would regional customers receive a practical repair and support route?

oneLine: Explore a large mining payload through an Earth-based systems study with visible assumptions.
need: A large launch vehicle does not by itself create a viable off-world mine. A payload would need to reach a selected destination, understand its material, operate equipment, manage power and handle its output. Each unresolved step can change the entire enterprise case.
offer: Develop a mission-design workbench for one proposed mining task. Retain the source's Starship-scale ambition as a design scenario while making vehicle interfaces, mission availability and partnerships explicitly unconfirmed. Start with a harmless terrestrial material-handling analogue and a transparent mass-and-power budget.
users: Space systems students and research teams
Robotics developers studying remote material handling
Founders comparing a component opportunity with a complete mining mission

firstPilot.title: A small analogue of one mining operation
steps: Select a single task such as collecting and transferring a known substitute material.
Write the proposed mission environment and separate known inputs from assumptions.
Build or simulate the handling sequence with an engineering supervisor.
Record material moved, equipment interruptions and power use where measurable.
Update the mission model and identify the assumption that most changes its viability.

businessModel: Small-batch apparel, pattern licensing or specialist design services, with inclusive fit work included in the actual production model.
leadershipDecision: Let participants choose whether they want practical, glamorous or blended styling. Do not use body diversity only in advertising while retaining narrow sizing.
risks: A small fit sample may miss important body differences.
Privacy can be compromised by unnecessary images or measurements.
Manufacturing costs can undermine an advertised size range.
equalityQuestions: Can women with very large busts, implants or larger bodies lead design decisions?
Can privacy and attractive styling coexist with practical support and affordability?

oneLine: Co-design an Aura support tool around a disabled person's chosen task and control.
need: An AI assistant can sound helpful while making assumptions about what a disabled person needs. A useful concept begins with the person's own goals, communication preferences and right to choose support. It should remove a practical burden without becoming another system they must explain themselves to.
offer: Develop a non-clinical, participant-led assistant prototype for one everyday task such as organising a chosen activity or preparing questions for a service meeting. Use fictional information first and make a human support option available in the design. The title does not imply NDIS approval, funding or a provider relationship.
users: Disabled adults who choose to help design a tool
Support organisations investigating a specific administrative barrier
Developers learning participant-led accessibility practice

firstPilot.title: One task chosen by the participant
steps: Pay participant advisers to choose a useful task and define what control means.
Build a simple prototype with the communication formats they request.
Test using fictional records before considering personal information.
Make correction, refusal, deletion and a non-AI route easy to use.
Ask participants whether the tool reduced effort and respected their choices.
firstPilot.deliverable: An accessible prototype, participant-reviewed findings and a clear statement of its limits.

evidence.known: A limited accessibility prototype can be co-designed and evaluated. It is not a clinical service or confirmed funded support.
evidence.unknown: No participant arrangement, provider, funding pathway, live AI system or evaluated benefit is established.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Compare the participant-defined effort and independence involved in the selected task.

resources: Paid disabled co-designers
An accessibility specialist and developer
Appropriate human support and accessible testing formats
businessModel: Commissioned accessibility design or a clearly scoped tool service, with payment arrangements explored without assuming entitlement.
leadershipDecision: Give disabled participants authority over the problem and success criteria, including the decision that AI is not useful for the task.
risks: A persona can appear more capable than the service behind it.
Supporters may speak over the person's own preferences.
An automated suggestion can create extra administrative work.
equalityQuestions: Can disabled women direct the design and retain control over their information?
Is a human or non-digital option equally available?

oneLine: Explore AI assistance that supports older people's preferences and the people caring alongside them.
need: Older women have varied abilities, histories and ambitions. An assistant should not assume that age means loneliness, poor technical skill or a desire for constant monitoring. A useful service begins with one chosen task and asks whether it makes daily life easier without reducing privacy or human contact.
offer: Co-design a non-clinical Aura prototype for a task such as preparing an activity plan, finding an approved document or organising questions for a care conversation. Involve older people directly and include supporters only with their agreement. Use fictional information in the first test.
users: Older adults choosing to shape a practical tool
Care organisations examining a specific administrative burden
Families and supporters seeking clearer coordination

firstPilot.title: A useful task, chosen by the older person
steps: Invite paid older participant advisers with varied technical confidence and access needs.
Choose a task and agree what the assistant should remember, if anything.
Prototype large, clear controls with text, audio or other requested formats.
Test corrections and interruptions using fictional records.
Review whether the tool supports the person's agency and leaves time for human connection.
firstPilot.deliverable: A participant-reviewed prototype and a defined service question for further testing.

evidence.known: A bounded usability study can explore an administrative or social task. It does not establish clinical benefit or a care service.
evidence.unknown: The source confirms no provider, live system, staffing arrangement, funding pathway or evaluated outcome.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Ask participants to complete the chosen task and explain how to correct or clear the assistant's information.

resources: Paid older co-designers
An accessibility designer and developer
Appropriate care-sector reviewers and accessible testing space
businessModel: Co-design, training or a narrowly scoped support tool, with ongoing human assistance and maintenance included in any offer.
leadershipDecision: Make the older person's preferences authoritative, including the choice not to use the tool or not to share information with others.
risks: Supporters may prioritise convenience over the person's wishes.
A friendly persona can imply care or availability that does not exist.
A tool may displace contact instead of freeing time for it.
equalityQuestions: Do older women have decision-making roles rather than only being depicted as recipients?
Can people refuse monitoring and still receive useful support?

oneLine: Support women returning from prison through participant-led learning, practical access and accountable human relationships.
need: A rehabilitation concept can become paternalistic if it defines success without the women involved. Returning to community life may involve work, housing, family, service navigation and the chance to be seen beyond a conviction. A useful venture should ask which practical barrier women want help addressing.
offer: Develop a proposed re-entry learning and navigation service with experienced community organisations and paid lived-experience advisers. Begin with a fictional service journey and one practical resource. AI, if used at all, would assist clearly bounded tasks rather than assess risk, determine eligibility or replace human support.
users: Women with lived experience of imprisonment who choose to participate
Community organisations providing re-entry support
Employers or educators examining a specific access barrier

firstPilot.title: One practical return-to-community pathway
steps: Invite paid lived-experience advisers through an appropriate willing organisation.
Let advisers choose a task such as understanding a training route or preparing for an appointment.
Map current information and identify where people must repeat their story.
Test a resource using fictional situations and voluntary feedback.
Give advisers approval over any public findings and identify the human service responsible for follow-through.
firstPilot.deliverable: A participant-reviewed resource and a clearly assigned next service improvement.

evidence.known: A community organisation can co-design practical learning and navigation resources. This proposal establishes no correctional programme or measured rehabilitation result.
evidence.unknown: No partner, participant access, service capacity, programme authority or evaluated outcome is confirmed.
evidence.nextMeasurement: Check whether the selected resource helps users complete the chosen task without unnecessary disclosure.

resources: Paid lived-experience advisers
An experienced re-entry organisation and facilitator
Current service information and clear human responsibility
businessModel: Commissioned community service design or supported learning programmes, with participant benefit and fair pay central to the model.
leadershipDecision: Give women with lived experience real power over the service and their stories. Separate support from surveillance and automated judgement.
risks: Participation may feel compulsory if authority relationships are unclear.
Public storytelling can expose personal history people wish to keep private.
A resource may point to services without available capacity.
equalityQuestions: Can women choose what history to disclose and what future to pursue?
Does the pathway address care, housing and transport rather than demanding motivation alone?
